chapters.title: Scan a million rows or four?

scenes.say: Finding one user among a million rows should not mean reading all of them. By the end, you'll make it read four, and spot the hidden fifty one queries behind a blog page.
Today you will do three things. Make a lookup read four rows instead of a million. Know when an index backfires. And spot and fix the hidden fifty one queries.
lines: Spot and fix the N+1 queries

scenes.title: Why is this lookup slow?
scenes.statement: A users table has a million rows. Finding one user by email takes far too long.
scenes.say: Here's the problem. A million rows, and finding one email is slow. For example, one email among a million users. We want to read about four rows, not a million.

scenes.head: Same lookup, a million users
scenes.say: Same lookup, a million users, on my laptop. Scanning every row takes seventy milliseconds. With an index, three hundredths. Two thousand times faster, same answer.

scenes.head: A catalog for your table
scenes.say: Picture a library with a million books and no catalog. To find one title, you walk every shelf. That's a full table scan. Now add a catalog: look up the title, read a shelf number, walk straight there. The catalog is the index.

scenes.head: A B-tree finding user 50
scenes.say: The catalog is usually a B tree: keys kept sorted. We want user fifty. The root page holds thirty and sixty. Below it sit three children, one for each range. Fifty is between thirty and sixty, so we take the middle one. It holds forty and fifty, plus a pointer to the row. Real pages hold hundreds of keys, so ten million rows need only three or four steps down.

scenes.head: No index: scan
scenes.say: I'm using SQLite. Ask it how it will run this lookup. Explain query plan prints the plan. No index exists, so it says scan users. Postgres calls that a Seq Scan.

setup.seed.sql:
CREATE TABLE users(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT, name TEXT, country TEXT, city TEXT);
WITH RECURSIVE c(i) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT i+1 FROM c WHERE i<1000) INSERT INTO users(email,name,country,city) SELECT 'user'||i||'@mail.com','n'||i,CASE i%2 WHEN 0 THEN 'DE' ELSE 'FR' END,'city'||(i%50) FROM c;

scenes.head: Add the index: search
scenes.say: Add one line. Create index builds the sorted tree on email. Same lookup again. Now the plan says search, using the index. Postgres calls that an Index Scan.

scenes.say: Your turn. The index is on email only. One of these filters cannot use it. Which one? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Index on `email`. Which filter can NOT use it?

scenes.head: Three lookups, three plans
scenes.say: The lower one. A function hides the sorted order, so it scans. A leading wildcard scans too, since the tree is sorted from the first letter. A plain range is fine. The fix: an index on lower of email.
That answers our problem. An index turns a scan of a million rows into a few steps.
lines: Index: a few steps, not a scan

scenes.title: When does an index backfire?
scenes.statement: Indexes speed up reads, but every write pays for them. Which indexes help, and which hurt?

example.output: index only what you filter, join, sort

scenes.say: Next problem. Indexes speed up reads, but every write pays for them. For example, a table with three indexes and one insert. We want to know which indexes earn their cost.

scenes.head: Every index is extra work
scenes.say: Picture a team that indexes every column, to be safe. Now one insert arrives. The row goes into the table. It also goes into the email index. And into the name index. One insert, three writes. Every extra index repeats it, and costs disk too.

scenes.head: Rows an index lookup must fetch
scenes.say: Filter by email: one row comes back. Filter by city, one of fifty: a million divided by fifty, twenty thousand rows. Filter by country, two values: half a million. An index helps little there.

scenes.head: A phone book is a composite index
scenes.say: A phone book is sorted by last name, then first name. Every Smith sits together, so that lookup is fast. Every John? Scattered across every surname: read it all. A composite index behaves the same: leftmost column first.
Your turn. A composite index on country, then city. You filter only by city. Does the database use it? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Index on `(country, city)`. Query: `WHERE city = 'city7'`. Used?

scenes.head: Skip the leftmost column
scenes.say: No: a full scan. The index starts with country, and this filter skips it. So put the column you always filter by first.

setup.seed.sql:
CREATE TABLE users(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT, name TEXT, country TEXT, city TEXT);
WITH RECURSIVE c(i) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT i+1 FROM c WHERE i<1000) INSERT INTO users(email,name,country,city) SELECT 'user'||i||'@mail.com','n'||i,CASE i%2 WHEN 0 THEN 'DE' ELSE 'FR' END,'city'||(i%50) FROM c;

scenes.head: Why a B-tree, not a hash?
scenes.say: Why a B tree? Equality works in both. Ranges need sorted order, and a hash has none. Order by wants sorted output. So index what you filter, join or sort on.
That answers it. An index costs writes, so index what you filter, join or sort on.

scenes.title: Why does one page run 51 queries?
scenes.statement: A blog page shows 50 posts with author names, and it is slow. Find out why, and fix it.
scenes.say: Next problem. A blog page shows fifty posts with author names, and it is slow. For example, fifty posts, each with an author. We want two queries, not fifty one.

scenes.head: A shopping trip
scenes.say: Your blog page shows fifty posts, each with an author name. Picture shopping for fifty items. Fifty trips, one item each? Or one trip with a list? Each trip costs the drive. A database query costs a round trip.

scenes.head: One blog page, many queries
scenes.say: Here's what the page does. First, one query loads fifty posts. That's one. Then, for each post, it asks for the author. Post one, post two, all the way to fifty. That's fifty one queries. At two milliseconds a round trip, that's a hundred and two milliseconds.

scenes.head: The bug, in code
scenes.say: Here it is as code. One query loads the posts. Then a loop asks for each author, one at a time. That loop body runs fifty times. The print shows how many queries ran: fifty one.

panels.code:
posts = query("SELECT * FROM posts LIMIT 50")
for p in posts:
    query("SELECT * FROM authors WHERE id = ?",
          p["author_id"])
print(calls)

setup.app.py:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
db.executescript("CREATE TABLE authors(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT); CREATE TABLE posts(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT, author_id INT);")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO authors VALUES (?,?)", [(i, "a%d" % i) for i in range(1, 11)])
db.executemany("INSERT INTO posts VALUES (?,?,?)", [(i, "p%d" % i, i % 10 + 1) for i in range(1, 51)])
calls = 0
def query(sql, *args):
    global calls
    calls += 1
    return db.execute(sql, args).fetchall()

scenes.say: Your turn. Those fifty posts have only ten different authors. A batched in query fetches the authors all at once. How many queries now? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: 50 posts, 10 distinct authors. Batched `IN` fix: how many queries?

scenes.head: Fix one: batch with IN
scenes.say: Two: the posts, then all ten authors in one go. First, collect the distinct ids. Then one placeholder per id builds the list. A single query fetches every author. The counter prints two.

panels.code:
posts = query("SELECT * FROM posts LIMIT 50")
ids = list({p["author_id"] for p in posts})
slots = ", ".join(["?"] * len(ids))
query(f"SELECT * FROM authors WHERE id IN ({slots})", *ids)
print(calls)

scenes.head: Fix two: let the database join
scenes.say: Or let the database join them. A join glues each post to the author row with the matching id. One query. The counter prints one.

panels.code:
rows = query("""SELECT p.title, a.name
    FROM posts p
    JOIN authors a ON a.id = p.author_id
    LIMIT 50""")
print(calls)

scenes.head: Join or batch?
scenes.say: Most frameworks do both for you. Django's select related is a join: one query, but the author repeats on every post row. Prefetch related is the in query: two queries, each row once. Rails includes picks between the two. Either way, never query inside a loop.
That answers it. Join or batch, and the fifty one queries become one or two.

scenes.title: A page is slow. Where do we start?
scenes.statement: Someone says add an index. How do we find the real cause before changing anything?

example.output: find it, fix one thing, measure

scenes.say: Last problem. A page is slow, and someone says add an index. For example, a slow page with no known cause. We want to find the real cause, fix one thing, and measure.

scenes.head: Slow page? Follow the order
scenes.say: A teammate says the page is slow, so add an index. Wait. First, count the queries per request. Fifty identical ones means N plus one. Next, read the plan of the slowest query. Fix one thing. Then measure again.

scenes.head: Read the plan
scenes.say: On Postgres, explain analyze runs the query and prints its plan. A Seq Scan on a big table with a filter is the red flag. An Index Scan means the tree is working. And estimated rows far from actual rows means out of date statistics, so run analyze.
rows: the sorted tree is in use

scenes.say: Your turn. A table has twenty rows, and the plan shows a Seq Scan. Should you add an index? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: 20-row table, plan shows Seq Scan. Add an index?

scenes.head: Pages read on a 20-row table
scenes.say: No. Twenty rows fit on one page, so a scan reads one. An index reads its own page, then the table page: at least two. Tiny tables don't need one. Measure first.
That answers it. Count the queries, read the plan, fix one thing, measure.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: How does an index help? Sorted B tree: a few steps, not a scan. When do indexes hurt? Every write updates every index. Composite index? Leftmost column first. How do you check? Explain, before and after.
rows: Sorted B-tree: a few steps, no full scan

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What's N plus one? A query per row: fifty one for fifty posts. The fix? A join, or one batched in query. Spotting it? Count queries per request. Is Seq Scan always bad? No, not on tiny tables. Measure first.
rows: A query per row: 51 for 50 posts

scenes.head: Do this tonight
scenes.say: Try three things. Add an index on email, and compare explain before and after. Then wrap the column in lower, and watch the index stop working. Finally, count the queries on one page of your own app, and fix the loop.
So say this. An index is a sorted tree: a few hops instead of a scan. It costs writes, so index what you filter and sort on. And N plus one is a query in a loop: join, batch, measure.
lines: An index is a sorted tree: few steps, no scan.
It costs writes: index what you filter and sort.
N+1 is a query in a loop: join, batch, measure.
